title: Injectable Senolytic Hydrogel Depot for the Clearance of Senescent Cells

sections.abstract: Small molecules are frontline therapeutics for many diseases; however, they are often limited by their poor solubility. Therefore, hydrophobic small molecules are often encapsulated or prepared as pure drug nanoparticles. Navitoclax, used to eliminate senescent cells, is one such small molecule that faces challenges in translation due to its hydrophobicity and toxic side effects. Further, as senescent cells exhibit context-dependent pathologic or beneficial properties, it is preferable to eliminate senescent cells locally. To formulate navitoclax and enable local treatment, we designed an injectable hydrogel loaded with navitoclax nanoparticles as a senolytic delivery vehicle. Navitoclax nanoparticles (Ø ∼ 110 nm) were prepared via solvent–antisolvent nanoprecipitation and formulated in an injectable polymer–nanoparticle (PNP) hydrogel to create a local senolytic depot. Navitoclax-loaded PNP hydrogels selectively cleared senescent cells in vitro in senescent endothelial monolayers. This work demonstrates the value of formulating lipophilic small molecules and the potential of localized drug delivery strategies to improve senolytic therapies.
sections.introduction:
Modern medical advances rely on the development of novel drug compounds to correct underlying pathological conditions. 1 , 2 While many emerging therapeutics are biologics, artificial intelligence and our growing knowledge of disease pathogenesis led to newly developed or repurposed small molecule therapeutics that are accessible, chemically stable, cost-effective, and easy to manufacture. 3 However, hydrophobic small molecules often have a limited bioavailability and formulation strategies are needed to enhance their effectiveness. 4 − 11 Crystalline or amorphous nanoparticles of pure drug allow increased drug loading while maintaining the advantages of nanotherapeutics, such as facilitated transport, avoided clearance, and increased dissolution kinetics. 12 − 14 The main drawback of hydrophobic small molecule therapeutics is their tendency to aggregate and form agglomerates, which are challenging to inject. This motivates the need to identify suitable biomaterial strategies to safely load and apply pure drug nanoparticles for therapeutic applications.

One emerging area in which small molecules are being developed for clinical application are senolytics, which are drugs that are designed to eliminate senescent cells and increase lifespan. 15 − 19 Senescent cells are growth-arrested cells that accumulate in tissues and organs with age, often impairing tissue function and regeneration. These cells often contribute to the development of age-related diseases where loss of proliferation-competent cells may be responsible for pathology, as in glaucoma, atherosclerosis, and osteoarthritis. 20 , 21 Senescent cells exhibit dysfunctions in B-cell lymphoma family proteins (Bcl-2, Bcl-xL, and Bcl-w), which prevents them from undergoing apoptosis. 22 , 23 Bcl-2 inhibitors, such as navitoclax (previously known as ABT-263), are hydrophobic small molecules that can act as senolytics by removing a block to apoptosis. 24 Navitoclax has been used to target senescence in the cardiovascular system, successfully eliminating both senescent cardiomyocytes and endothelial cells, which can impair tissue regeneration and promote atherosclerosis, myocardial infarction, and cardiac fibrosis. 25 − 27 The elimination of senescent endothelial cells is associated with the formation of new blood vessels, and tissue reoxygenation and revitalization. 28 , 29 The effect of senolytics is widely studied; however, their formulation remains challenging and biomaterial carriers for senolytics are lacking.

While the clearance of senescent cells is beneficial to restore tissue homeostasis, senescent cells also act as essential tumor suppressors, for example via immunosurveillance, and should be preserved in certain contexts making it preferable to engineer local delivery strategies. 30 − 35 An additional challenge limiting the use of navitoclax as a senolytic is its low solubility in aqueous media and thrombocytopenia, which is its primary dose-limiting toxicity. 36 − 39 Current in vitro formulations dissolve navitoclax in dimethyl sulfoxide prior to adding this solution directly to the cell culture medium. 40 In animal models, navitoclax is formulated with lipids and administered orally in a high dose, since absorption through the gastrointestinal tract is limited. 36 Other strategies have focused on chemically modifying navitoclax to increase its solubility and specificity to senescent cells and reduce thrombocytopenia. 41 , 42 These formulation strategies improve the targeting of senescent cells and decrease platelet toxicity, but their systemic delivery may result in senescent cell death in locations where they have beneficial effects, i.e., tumor suppression. The formation of local drug depots containing pure senolytic nanoparticles would affect mainly neighboring tissue areas and resolve limitations associated with systemic administration. 43

We repurposed an established supramolecular drug delivery system, polymer–nanoparticle (PNP) hydrogels, by using it for the stabilization and delivery of pure navitoclax nanoparticles to form injectable biomaterials for the local eradication of senescent cells. 44 − 46 We prepared the navitoclax nanoparticles using solvent–antisolvent nanoprecipitation, forming controlled spherical pure drug nanoparticles. When applied to healthy and senescent human umbilical vein endothelial cell (HUVEC) monolayers, navitoclax nanoparticles were more selective in eliminating senescent HUVECs than the direct addition of navitoclax to the culture medium, significantly improving monolayer proliferation rates. This shifted the therapeutic window to lower concentrations. We further formulated navitoclax nanoparticles into PNP hydrogels to form an injectable senolytic-loaded hydrogel depot ( Figure 1 a). The navitoclax-nanoparticle-loaded PNP hydrogels promoted monolayer regeneration. Overall, this work demonstrates that supramolecular hydrogels are suitable carriers for pure drug nanoparticles, allowing application without reformulation and enabling local administration of senolytics, thereby addressing open problems in clinical translation.

Local injectable hydrogel loaded with controlled navitoclax nanoparticles. (a) Accumulation of senescent cells often leads to impaired tissue function. We designed polymer–nanoparticle (PNP) hydrogels loaded with navitoclax nanoparticles that can be applied via injection with the aim of eliminating senescent cells. (b) The current standard formulation involves direct addition of navitoclax to aqueous media resulting in uncontrolled particle production. Therefore, we produced navitoclax nanoparticles using a solvent–antisolvent nanoprecipitation for controlled particle production. (c) Size of nanoparticles with current standard formulation and controlled nanoprecipitation. (d) Dispersity index of the nanoparticles in each formulation method. (e) Controlled navitoclax nanoparticles remained stable in aqueous media at room temperature (25 ° C) for up to 15 days.
sections.methods:
Navitoclax nanoparticles were formed via controlled nanoprecipitation without excipients. Navitoclax (MedChem Express, C 47 H 55 ClF 3 N 5 O 6 S 3 , 974.61 g mol –1 ) was dissolved in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO, VWR) at a concentration of 5 mg mL –1 . 50 μL were added dropwise to 500 μL of deionized water while stirring with a magnetic stir bar (350 rpm; 25 °C). We determined the nanoparticle size by dynamic light scattering using Malvern Zetasizer Nano ZS. Nanoparticle suspensions were diluted 10-fold with deionized water in a disposable Malvern polystyrene semimicro cuvette (Braun). Measurements were performed at room temperature at a scattering angle of 173°. Nanoparticle hydrodynamic diameters, D h , and particle dispersities, Đ , are reported as mean ± standard deviation of three independent experiments and three DLS measurements per sample.

Human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs; PromoCell, C-12203, pooled donors) were cultured in a medium containing 80% Endothelial Cell Growth Medium (PromoCell, C-22010) with SupplementMix (PromoCell, C-39215), and 20% FBS (ThermoFisher A3160801). Cells were grown at 37 °C and 5% CO 2 and detached with Accutase (Thermofisher, A11105-01) for splitting. All culture substrates were coated with a 1.5 wt % sterile gelatin (Merck, 90000-70-80) solution prior to cell seeding. Inflammatory senescence was induced by adapting a protocol from Chala et al. 39 Cells were seeded at 5 × 10 3 cells cm –2 and cultured for 12 days. Every second day the cell culture medium was exchanged with fresh medium supplemented with 10 ng mL –1 of TNF-α (#300-01A, PeproTech, Senescent group). For our experiments, unless specified, passages were kept below 10.

Cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (ThermoFisher, 28906) in DPBS (with Ca 2+ and Mg 2+ ) for 15 min at room temperature and permeabilized with Triton-X (Triton X-100, Sigma-Aldrich, 1002538787) 0.5 vol % for 10 min. Cells were then blocked with 5 wt % bovine serum albumin (BSA, Sigma-Aldrich, A2153-100g) for 1 h at room temperature (25 °C) and incubated overnight with primary antibodies at 4 °C. Subsequently, cells were washed 5 times with PBS (ThermoFisher, 10010-015) and incubated with secondary antibodies and nuclear staining for 45 min at room temperature (25 °C). The staining solutions used in this study are described in Table S1 .

Cells were then imaged with the THUNDER fluorescence microscope (Leica) with a 10× objective, NA 0.32. Images were further processed with computational clearing in a LAS X-Leica DMi8. The proliferative index was calculated as follows

Healthy and senescent cells were seeded in 96-well plates and treated with increasing concentrations of navitoclax in DMSO (0.1–100 μM, 0.6 vol % DMSO) or navitoclax nanoparticles formed via controlled nanoprecipitation (0.1–28 μM, 0.6 vol % DMSO) for 3 days. At the end of the treatment, cells were fixed and stained, and 5 images were acquired in different, nonoverlapping regions of each well. The total number of DAPI-stained nuclei per field of view were counted using a custom Matlab script. For every condition, the number of DAPI-stained nuclei was divided by the number of DAPI-stained nuclei of an untreated control (0 μM navitoclax, 0.6% DMSO) and the fraction was expressed in terms of percentages.

Results are reported as the mean ± standard deviation of three independent experiments. The half inhibitory concentration, IC50, was calculated by interpolating the experimental results to a logistic function ( eq 1 ). 47 1

Poly(ethylene glycol) 5k - block -polylactide 18k (PEG- b -PLA) was synthesized via stannous octoate-catalyzed ring-opening polymerization of lactide in the presence of 5 kDa methoxy PEG. 48 The reaction was conducted in an anhydrous and inert environment. Poly(ethylene glycol) methyl ether (5 kDa; 3.5 g, 0.7 mmol, Sigma-Aldrich) and 3,6-dimethyl-1,4-dioxane-2,5-dione (LA; 11.180 g, 77 mmol, Sigma-Aldrich) were dissolved in 30 mL of toluene and heated to 100 °C. Tin(II) 2-ethylhexanoate (0.32 mL, 0.9 mmol) was added to the PEG/LA/toluene mixture, and the temperature was increased to 140 °C for 6.5 h. The mixture was cooled to room temperature, and the polymer was recovered via precipitation in ice-cold diethyl ether, filtration, and vacuum drying for 2 days. The product was characterized via NMR and size-exclusion chromatography.

To make PEG- b -PLA nanoparticles, 140 mg of PEG- b -PLA was dissolved in 2.5 mL of acetone. Using an electronic pipet (LTS E4-1000 XLS+, Mettler-Toledo), the polymer solution was added in 15 μL droplets to 10 mL of deionized water under magnetic stirring at 700 rpm. The residual acetone evaporated at ambient temperature. The NP solution was centrifuged at 4500 rcf for 70 min using 50 kDa Amicon Ultra-15 Centrifugal Filter Units (Merck Millipore) and resuspended to 20 wt % using deionized water.

PNP hydrogels were formed by mixing a solution containing hydroxypropylmethylcellulose (HPMC, M n ∼ 700 kDa, Sigma-Aldrich) with one containing PEG- b -PLA nanoparticles. Four mg HPMC were dissolved overnight in a syringe with 96 mg PBS in the case of nondrug-loaded PNP hydrogels, while for navitoclax-loaded PNP hydrogels 4 mg HPMC were dissolved in 96 mg navitoclax nanoparticle solution at 0.45 mg mL –1 . In a second syringe, 300 mg of a 20 wt % PEG- b -PLA nanoparticle solution in PBS was added (15 wt % of the total hydrogel). The two syringes were connected using a female-to-female Luer lock, and the liquids were mixed by repeatedly squeezing the formulation from one side to the other. The final navitoclax loading in the hydrogel was 0.11 mg mL –1 or 112 μM. The formed PNP hydrogels were left to equilibrate overnight at ambient temperature. For in vitro tests, senescent HUVECs were seeded in 24 well plates with 0.5 mL of culture media; a 3 μm pore size transwell (Corning) was placed on top of it, and 100 mg of PNP hydrogel, either loaded with navitoclax (0.11 mg mL –1 ) or not, were added.

Rheological measurements were performed on a shear rheometer (MCR 502, Anton Paar). All tests were performed using a 20 mm diameter parallel plate geometry with a measurement gap of 0.5 mm. Tests were conducted at 25 °C and silicon oil was pipetted at the edge of the geometry to prevent water evaporation. The linear viscoelastic regime was quantified by performing dynamic oscillatory strain amplitude measurements with a constant angular frequency of ω = 1.6 Hz. This frequency was confirmed to be within the linear viscoelastic regime. The frequency response of PNP hydrogel formulations was assessed with dynamic oscillatory frequency sweep measurements (ω = 16–0.002 Hz) at γ = 0.001%. Rotational shear rate measurements where δγ/δ t was increased from 0.01 to 100 s –1 were used to characterize the flow behavior of PNP hydrogel formulations. The linear range of the measured dynamic viscosity, η, was fit to power law model η = K PL (δγ/δ t ) n −1 , where n is the shear-thinning index and K PL is the consistency index. The ability of PNP hydrogels to recover their network properties after being sheared, self-healing behavior, was assessed by alternating intervals of low dynamic oscillatory strain (γ = 0.001%, ω = 1.6 Hz) to high oscillatory strain (γ = 5%, ω = 1.6 Hz).

PNP hydrogels with and without navitoclax nanoparticles were formed as described previously (Polymer–Nanoparticle Hydrogel Formation) and placed in Eppendorf tubes for a total of 100 mg of hydrogel per tube. In each tube, 0.5 mL of fresh PBS was added. Samples were then incubated at 37 °C in a shaking incubator at 120 rpm. Every 24 h, the supernatant was collected, frozen, and lyophilized (Lyovapor L-300 lyophilizer BUCHI Labortechnik AG, Flawil, Switzerland). The lyophilized mass was weighed and used to calculate the cumulative mass lost by using the following formula

Oil Red O was used as a model hydrophobic molecule to study drug release. PNP hydrogels loaded with Oil Red O nanoparticles were formed following the same procedure to form PNP hydrogels loaded with navitoclax nanoparticles. For most experiments, we used 15 wt % of PEG- b -PLA nanoparticles. The data in Figure S6 was acquired by tuning the PEG- b -PLA nanoparticle content to 7.5, 5, or 2.5 wt %. The release assay was performed by adding 100 mg PNP hydrogel with or without Oil Red O nanoparticles (0.11 mg mL –1 ) to the bottom of an Eppendorf tube and 0.5 mL of fresh PBS were added on top. Samples were stored at 37 °C in a shaking incubator at 120 rpm, and release was quantified after 6, 24, 48, 72, and 96 h.

At each time point, 0.250 mL of supernatant solution was collected from each sample and gently replaced with fresh PBS. The retrieved supernatant solution was then mixed with 0.250 mL of acetonitrile and sonicated for 10 min before analysis via UV–visible spectroscopy (λ abs = 520 nm). The amount of Oil Red O released was calculated based on calibration curves. To account for the background produced by the eroding PNP hydrogel, the absorption of the control PNP hydrogels was subtracted from absorption of Oil Red O nanoparticle-loaded hydrogels.

All results are presented as mean ± standard deviation, and paired sample t tests were used to assess significant differences in the means between conditions.
sections.results:
In vitro, navitoclax is generally dissolved in DMSO and added to the culture medium, which we refer to as current standard. 49 , 50 However, as navitoclax is hydrophobic (log P > 7.5), we observed that upon contact with the aqueous culture medium, navitoclax precipitates and forms heterogeneous particles with an average diameter of 480 ± 490 nm and a dispersity Đ = 0.43 ± 0.24 ( Figure 1 c). Based on this, we hypothesized that a controlled nanoprecipitation of navitoclax using a solvent–antisolvent method would prepare more uniform and effective nanoparticles ( Figure 1 b). Using this approach, spherical nanoparticles were formed with an average diameter of 110 ± 5 nm ( Figures 1 c and S1a ). The controlled nanoparticles were also more uniform, with a dispersity of Đ = 0.12 ± 0.02 ( Figures 1 d and S1b ). These nanoparticles were stable during storage when kept in solution (1:10 DMSO/water) with no change in diameter over a period of 15 days at room temperature (25 °C; Figure 1 e).

To mimic inflammation-induced senescence of the endothelium in vitro, HUVECs were chronically treated with a solution of TNF-α. 51 To quantify the induction of senescence we used the ratio of the proliferation marker Ki67 to the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p21, a marker of growth arrest, as quantified via immunocytochemistry and fluorescence imaging. 52 , 53 We used this ratio as a measure of the proliferative index, where a high value indicates an abundance of proliferating cells and a low value indicates an abundance of growth-arrested or senescent cells. TNF-α-treated cell populations exhibited a lower proliferative index (∼1.5) than healthy untreated populations (∼3.5) as well as a lower total number of cells, suggesting a higher number of nonproliferating cells, which is a known trait of cellular senescence ( Figures 2 a and S2a ). Moreover, TNF-α-induced senescent cells exhibited similar proliferative index as replicative senescent cells, obtained by expanding HUVECs for more than 15 passages, consistent with previous studies. 54 Other common traits of senescence were observed in TNF-α-treated HUVECs, such as enlarged morphology ( Figure S2b ) and increased expression of inflammatory genes hIL6 and hIL8 ( Figure S2c ). 55 Based on these data, we concluded that TNF-α treatment induced inflammation-based senescence in the HUVEC populations.

Improved selectivity of controlled navitoclax nanoparticles. (a) Senescence was quantified by staining for p21 and Ki67. TNF-α-treated HUVECs exhibited a higher percentage of Ki67 – p21 + cells, indicating a higher percentage of growth-arrested (senescent) cells in the treated population. Late passage HUVECs exhibited a similar phenotype. (b) IC50 curve of the current standard navitoclax administration for healthy and senescent populations showing similar behavior for the two HUVEC populations and limited selectivity. (c) IC50 curve of controlled navitoclax nanoparticles indicating a shift in sensitivity to the drug: the viability of senescent populations decreased at lower concentrations than healthy populations. (d) Quantification of cell number (DAPI) after treatment with no navitoclax (untreated) or current standard and navitoclax nanoparticles at 5 μM. Scale bar, 100 μm. *** p < 0.001, ** p < 0.01, and * p < 0.05.

We then investigated the efficacy of controlled navitoclax nanoparticles to eliminate senescent HUVECs compared with the current standard addition of free navitoclax in DMSO. As expected, the final number of healthy or senescent cells decreased with an increasing concentration of free navitoclax or controlled navitoclax nanoparticles ( Figure 2 b,c). No significant difference was observed in the half inhibitory concentration when healthy HUVECs or senescent HUVECs were treated with current standard navitoclax (IC50 = 9 and 10 μM, respectively). On the other hand, healthy and senescent cells responded differently to controlled navitoclax nanoparticles. Senescent cells were more sensitive to low navitoclax nanoparticle concentration (IC50 = 4 μM), whereas healthy cells remained viable at higher concentrations (IC50 = 16 μM; Figure 2 c). The difference in the percentage of viable cells for healthy and senescent cells [normalized to untreated (0.6% DMSO) populations] with 5 μM navitoclax was significantly larger for controlled navitoclax nanoparticles than current standard addition, indicating that nanoparticles selectively affected senescent cells ( Figure 2 d). The cell response was similar at 10 μM, which was closer to the IC50 value calculated for the current standard navitoclax treatment, corroborating the improved selectivity for senescent cells of controlled navitoclax nanoparticles ( Figure S2d ). Overall, controlled navitoclax nanoparticles selectively eliminated senescent cells more efficiently than healthy cells, providing a wider therapeutic window for the treatment of senescent cells without damaging healthy cells.

To further study whether navitoclax nanoparticles formed via solvent–antisolvent nanoprecipitation can restore the proliferative potential of senescent HUVECs, we performed recovery tests on cell monolayers. Senescent populations were either treated with navitoclax nanoparticles at 5 μM or with fresh media for 3 days; subsequently, cells were fixed and stained for p21 and Ki67 to calculate the proliferative index. As contact-inhibited cells also express p21, creating a bias in the proliferative indices, we performed the experiments in two different ways. 53 First, we did a recovery test in which the drug was removed after 3 days and cells were provided with fresh media for an additional 24 or 48 h ( Figure 3 a, left). In parallel, we also performed a reseeding recovery test in which cells were detached and reseeded at low densities onto new well plates after 3 days of drug treatment ( Figure 3 a, right) and allowed to recover for 24 or 48 h prior to staining. These are respectively reported as day 4 and 5 post-treatment start. In both experiments, cells treated with navitoclax nanoparticles exhibited a significantly higher proliferative index than untreated samples ( Figure 3 b–e). This suggests that controlled navitoclax nanoparticles were able to selectively eliminate senescent cells and allow the healthy cells within the population to proliferate and regenerate the monolayer.

Controlled navitoclax nanoparticles eliminate senescent cells facilitating monolayer regeneration. (a) Schematic illustration of recovery and reseeding recovery experiments. In the recovery experiment, cells were treated for 3 days. One set of samples was allowed to recover for 24 h in the same wells (plotted as Day 4 post-treatment start) and a second set of samples was allowed to recover for 48 h in the same wells (plotted as Day 5 post-treatment start). In the reseeding recovery experiment, cells were detached after treatment and reseeded into new wells. One set of samples was allowed to recover for 24 h in the new wells (plotted as Day 4 post-treatment start) and a second set of samples was allowed to recover for 48 h in the new well (plotted as Day 5 post-treatment start). (b–d) Immunofluorescence (IF) micrographs labeling nuclei (DAPI, blue), Ki67 (magenta), and p21 (red) of senescent cells untreated (control) or treated with controlled navitoclax nanoparticles and allowed to recover for 24 h or allowed to recover for 48 h without (b) or with reseeding (d) and quantification of the proliferative index after treatment with controlled navitoclax nanoparticles without (c) or with reseeding (e). Scale bars, 100 μm. *** p < 0.001.

Local elimination of senescent cells is preferred as they exhibit beneficial effects in certain contexts. 31 Thus, we engineered a biomaterial strategy to enable local delivery of navitoclax nanoparticles by creating navitoclax-loaded biomaterial depots ( Figure 4 ). PNP hydrogels self-assemble upon mixing PEG- b -PLA nanoparticles and HPMC ( Figure 4 a). 47 , 48 To test whether the inclusion of pure drug navitoclax nanoparticles in the hydrogel network altered the mechanical properties, of the hydrogel, namely, its shear-thinning and self-healing properties, we characterized the rheology of the navitoclax-nanoparticle-loaded PNP hydrogels ( Figure S3 ). The navitoclax-nanoparticle-loaded samples preserved their shear-thinning behavior ( Figure 4 b) and elastic recovery ( Figure 4 c). We investigated changes in the hydrogel mass over time to determine gel degradation and release. Both nonloaded PNP and navitoclax nanoparticle-loaded PNP hydrogels were found to lose approximately 10–25% of mass every day up to around 70% erosion at 96 h ( Figure 4 d), suggesting no significant effect of navitoclax nanoparticles on the erosion properties of the gel. We tried to quantify the release of navitoclax nanoparticles from PNP hydrogels using calorimetric, chromatography, and mass spectrometry methods; however, the quantification of navitoclax was challenging due to limited absorbance in the UV–visible spectrum, the low solubility of navitoclax in solvents, and clogging of equipment caused by the eroded hydrogel matter. Scanning electron microscopy images suggested that navitoclax NPs were present in the released supernatant and remained insoluble during sample preparation for chromatography ( Figure S4 ). We therefore repeated the same encapsulation and release experiments using nanoparticles made of Oil Red O, which is a small molecule with similar hydrophobicity to that of navitoclax that has an absorbance maximum at 518 nm, making its quantification possible with standard UV–visible spectrophotometers ( Figure 4 e). We found that each day 18–25% of the Oil Red O nanoparticle payload was released in the supernatant. We fitted the experimental data to the Ritger–Peppas equation for the description of solute release and found a diffusional exponent, n , of 1.1, which suggested that Oil Red O nanoparticles were released by non-Fickian transport ( Supplementary Methods, Figure S5, and Table S3 ). 56 , 57 Since the release kinetics of Oil Red O nanoparticles and the erosion kinetics of PNP hydrogels were similar, we hypothesized that the release was mainly erosion-driven and that the hydrophobic small molecule particles were released as the hydrogel matrix eroded. We investigated whether PNP hydrogels exhibited tunable release of Oil Red O nanoparticles. As PEG- b -PLA nanoparticles were a structural component of the PNP hydrogels, we reduced their percentage and observed increased release kinetics for Oil Red O nanoparticles with decreased PEG- b -PLA nanoparticle contents ( Figure S6 ).

Navitoclax-nanoparticle-loaded PNP hydrogels restore the regenerative potential of senescent HUVECs. (a) Schematic illustration of PNP hydrogels loaded with navitoclax nanoparticles. (b) PNP hydrogels with and without navitoclax nanoparticles exhibit similar viscosity profiles in rotational shear rate ramp experiments. (c) PNP hydrogels loaded with navitoclax nanoparticles recover their mechanical properties in step strain experiments; the high shear region is indicated by the shaded area. (d) Cumulative mass loss from PNP gels and navitoclax nanoparticle-loaded PNP gels (PNP–Navitoclax nanoparticles) over time suggests no significant effect of the drug payload on the physical properties of the gel over time. (e) Cumulative release of Oil Red nanoparticles over time. 100% corresponds to releasing the entire Oil Red O amount initially loaded in the hydrogel. (f) Immunofluorescence micrographs of senescent HUVECs without treatment (untreated), treated with PNP control hydrogels without navitoclax (PNP ctrl), or with PNP hydrogels loaded with navitoclax nanoparticles (PNP–N1 and PNP–N2). (g) Number of cells per field of view remaining after different treatments showing no significant decrease in overall cell number. (h) The proliferative index increased for senescent HUVECs treated with PNP hydrogels loaded with navitoclax nanoparticles. *** p < 0.001, ** p < 0.01. Scale bar, 100 μm.

To test whether PNP hydrogels with navitoclax nanoparticles maintained their ability to eliminate senescent cells and restore the regenerative potential of HUVEC populations, we treated senescent cells with either fresh media (untreated), unloaded PNP hydrogels (PNP ctrl), or navitoclax-nanoparticle-loaded PNP hydrogels (PNP–N1 and PNP–N2) for 3 days and then quantified the proliferative index. In the case of PNP hydrogels loaded with nanocrystals, we compared two treatment regimens: PNP–N1 in which the loaded hydrogel was placed in a transwell and was left unperturbed for the entire 3 days, while in the second case (PNP–N2) media was removed every day and fresh media was added. Corroborating the effect of controlled navitoclax nanoparticles, the cell number decreased upon treatment with navitoclax-loaded PNP hydrogels ( Figure 4 f,g). Moreover, treatment with both PNP–N1 and PNP–N2 resulted in a significant increase in the proliferative index ( Figure 4 f,h), suggesting again that senescent cells were eliminated, allowing the healthy fraction of the population to proliferate and regenerate the monolayer. The nonloaded hydrogel (PNP ctrl) showed no difference in the proliferative index, indicating that the beneficial effects of PNP–N1 and PNP–N2 were caused by the inclusion of navitoclax nanoparticles in the formulation ( Figure 4 h).

To further investigate the dynamics of the recovery experiments, we developed a simplified mathematical model of cell population dynamics. This model allowed us to estimate theoretical extreme values of the proliferation ratio Ki67/p21 ( Supplementary Methods ). We simulated the effect that selectively targeting senescent cells would have on the regeneration of a cellular population. We initialized the model with values for cell doubling time and fraction of cycling cells determined on healthy, low confluence monolayers ( Table S5 ). The initial number of senescent cells was based on the observed experimental values. The computed evolution curves for both healthy and senescent cell populations yielded a proliferation ratio lower than what was measured experimentally (below 1) but suggested that even a small transient increase in Ki67/p21 can be indicative of greater cell proliferation and of a higher fraction of healthy cells ( Supplementary Results and Figures S7–S9 ). To better replicate the conditions found in living organisms, we repeated the simulations at higher cell densities while maintaining the same fraction of senescent cells ( Figure S10 ). Due to higher total area occupancy of senescent cells, targeting the latter with navitoclax created more space for healthy cells to proliferate, leading to a relevant increase in the proportion of healthy cells ( Figures S10e–h and S11 ). The phase diagram of the proliferation ratio of Ki67/p21 illustrates the interplay between cellular senescence and endothelial contact inhibition ( Figure 5 ). Targeting senescent cells and lowering contact inhibition drives the proliferation ratio to values ≥2. These simulation results modeled the system at carrying capacity and explained theoretically how navitoclax drives regeneration of a healthy endothelial monolayer by clearing of senescence cells and lowering contact inhibition.

Phase Diagram of the Proliferation Ratio Ki67 + /p21 + as a function of the area of healthy (horizontal axis) and senescent cells (vertical axis). Our simplified population balance model suggests that navitoclax treatment reduced senescence and contact inhibition, leading to higher proliferation ratios and improved endothelial monolayer regeneration.
sections.discussion:
Crystalline and amorphous hydrophobic small molecule nanoparticles enhance drug loading while preserving the benefits of nanotherapeutics, including improved transport, reduced clearance, and accelerated dissolution kinetics. 12 − 14 We used supramolecular PNP hydrogels to form local drug depots of pure navitoclax nanoparticles, a potent hydrophobic senolytic drug that is associated with systemic off-target effects and toxicity. 58

The nanoprecipitated particles were in the 100 nm range ( Figures 1 and S1 ), remained shelf-stable, and prevented uncontrolled drug precipitation that usually occurs with other formulation methods. The navitoclax nanoparticles maintained their senolytic activity and demonstrated higher efficiency and specificity toward senescent cells than the standard navitoclax formulation; the half-maximal inhibitory concentration was reduced from 10 to 5 μM ( Figure 2 b–d) suggesting that it is possible to achieve similar therapeutic effects while using a lower dosage and potentially mitigate side effects. We hypothesize that the reduction in particle diameter and distribution could play a role in the increased selectivity and efficiency observed for navitoclax nanoparticles produced in this study. 8 , 59 , 60 Other studies have shown similar results, where hydrophobic, small and similar-sized particles facilitated endocytosis. 8 , 59 , 60

Furthermore, we evaluated whether navitoclax treatment and senescent cell eradication could enable tissue regeneration, using TNF-α-treated senescent HUVEC monolayers as a model system. Our nanoformulated drug treatment cleared senescent cells and allowed healthy cells to proliferate and reform a stable HUVEC monolayer as demonstrated by the increase in the ratio of Ki67 + /p21 + cells ( Figure 3 b−d). In the untreated condition, there was no cell clearance, meaning that the senescent population remained viable, and the healthy cell population could not proliferate due to contact inhibition and remained subjected to the secretome of senescent cells. In the navitoclax-treated condition, we showed that the increase in proliferation ratio was due both to the loss of senescent cells, and to the proliferation of healthy cells, which were no longer contact-inhibited ( Figure 3 d,e). Overall, these results suggest that navitoclax treatment leads to monolayer regeneration, which is encouraging for its potential use in cardiovascular tissues.

In vascular tissues, senescent cells should be eliminated since they limit the formation of new blood vessels and impede tissue revitalization. However, there are cases in which senescent cells are beneficial since they locally act as tumor suppressors. 30 − 35 To avoid systemic clearance of senescent cells, we loaded controlled navitoclax particles in a biomaterial scaffold to form an injectable therapeutic depot that could be used in the future to eliminate senescent cells locally. We utilized established supramolecular PNP hydrogels, as they can be easily extruded through syringes and catheters while restoring their original mechanical properties and forming a depot postextrusion. In this study, we tested their capacity for stabilizing, loading, and releasing pure drug nanoparticles. The loading of pure drug nanoparticles did not interfere with the rheological and erosion properties of PNP hydrogels ( Figures 4 a–d and S3 ). The hydrogels exhibited an erosion profile ( Figure 4 d) that was similar to the release profile of Oil Red O nanoparticles, which were easier to analytically quantify ( Figure 4 e). SEM images and data fitting to the Ritger−Peppas equation suggested that the drug nanoparticles are released via erosion, together with the eroded hydrogel matrix. We analyzed the capacity of our navitoclax-loaded PNP hydrogels to act as senolytics and both conditions tested, PNP–N1 and PNP–N2, that differ solely in the timing of media change, partially restored the proliferative potential of the endothelial monolayer ( Figure 4 f–h). Since the experimental conditions tested in the drug release experiment resemble the ones of PNP−N2, we could infer that the navitoclax concentration in the cell culture medium was between 1 and 10 μM. The proliferation ratio of Figure 4 f was similar to the one of Figure 3 where a similar concentration of pure navitoclax nanoparticles was used. This could suggest that the activity of PNP-released navitoclax nanoparticles is similar to the one of pure drug nanoparticles; however, precise quantification of navitoclax in the cell culture medium is necessary to prove this hypothesis.

We have also developed a simplified mathematical model based on cell population dynamics, where we have modeled the effect of cellular senescence and endothelial contact inhibition on the proliferation ratio ( Supplementary Results and Figure 5 ). These theoretical results corroborate our experimental data where navitoclax-treated cells have increased proliferation ratios and highlight the importance of developing therapies that restore regeneration in tissues where senescence is unwanted.

Local treatments are beneficial for mitigating the adverse effects of the drug by reducing the concentration of the drug and affecting only the pathological tissue. The PNP formulation could become useful in treating cardiovascular pathologies or other tissues with resident senescent populations. Our platform could enable researchers to locally deplete senescent cells in the perspective of further unraveling the link between aging and senescence and developing interventions to promote healthy aging and extend lifespan. Since small molecule drug nanoparticles did not interfere with the rheological properties of the materials, injectable PNP hydrogels, or similar supramolecular biomaterials, could become a general carrier for navitoclax or other solid drug nanoparticles that are otherwise challenging to administer. The design of a generic carrier for solid drug nanoparticles could also simplify approval by regulatory agencies.
sections.conclusion: With our approach, we prepared stable navitoclax nanoparticles and demonstrated their efficacy in clearing senescence in a monolayer of HUVECs. We then embedded the nanoparticles within an injectable PNP hydrogel. The hydrogel scaffolds were suitable local drug depots for navitoclax, and they retained their senolytic effect, without significant alterations of the biomaterial scaffold properties. A simplified mathematical model further explained the combined effect of navitoclax on senescent cell clearance and contact inhibition. Our platform is promising for advancing localized treatments that selectively target senescent cells, offering a versatile and regulatory-friendly solution for addressing aging-related pathologies, promoting healthy aging, and potentially extending a healthy lifespan.
